# ADR-0014: Caches as decorators, no virtual filesystem

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-29

**References:** [ADR-0004](../adr/ADR-0004.md), [RFC-0002:C-PROJECTION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-projection), [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-preview), [RFC-0004:C-CACHE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-cache), [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host), [RFC-0004:C-INTEGRITY](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-integrity), [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding), [RFC-0006:C-LAYERING](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-layering), [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake), [RFC-0007:C-INVALIDATION](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-invalidation)

## Context

Asking where caching lives exposed that the question has no single answer. Four caches exist with different
keys, lifetimes and consequences: raw byte ranges keyed by source and offset; decoded batches keyed by node;
the consolidated edit overlay from [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake); and retained render state under
[RFC-0007:C-INVALIDATION](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-invalidation) 1. Treating them as one facility would give the least trustworthy of them the reach of
the most.

Placement followed from existing obligations rather than needing new ones. Byte-range and node caches belong
to the spatial access component, which already owns index traversal; the baked overlay belongs where edits are
evaluated; render state belongs to the rendering component, which [RFC-0006:C-LAYERING](../rfc/RFC-0006.md#rfc-0006c-layering) 3 keeps downstream
of both.

The proposal that caching needs a virtual filesystem to handle constrained hosts and reduce attack surface
turned out to invert the actual relationship. A filesystem abstraction means paths, directory traversal,
seekable handles and permissions — strictly *more* authority than caching requires. The two host interfaces
already in force are the minimal capability set: read a byte range from a named source, and put, get or delete
by opaque key with no in-place modification ([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 1 and 2). That narrowness is itself the
security property, since a keyed store with no paths has no path to traverse and a write-once store cannot be
modified between check and use. The decision behind [RFC-0004](../rfc/RFC-0004.md) had already recorded growth toward a general
filesystem as a drift to watch, so this was a case of the governance catching the question.

A structural observation simplified the byte cache: because retrieval is defined as explicit offset and length
with batched multi-range support, a cache *is* an implementation of that interface wrapping another, not a
layer beside it. Request coalescing and deduplication become portable logic while the backing store stays
host-supplied.

[RFC-0002:C-PROJECTION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-projection) creates a keying problem. An entry decoded for the
attributes one pipeline reads cannot serve a pipeline reading one further attribute, so keying on requested
projection fragments the cache per distinct projection, while keying on the whole record discards the benefit
projection exists for.

The genuine gap was integrity rather than capability. [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 5 detects a *stale* entry, not a
*modified* one, and a cache in shared storage can be altered by something other than this software. The
consequences are not uniform: a tampered baked overlay would change a delivered result while
[RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 2 asserts baking cannot change results, and a corrupted cached byte range feeding a
committed run changes output silently.

## Decision

Caches are decorators over the host interfaces already specified, keyed per attribute, and integrity-verified
only where an entry contributes to a committed run. The obligations are written in
[RFC-0004:C-CACHE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-cache) and [RFC-0004:C-INTEGRITY](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-integrity); this ADR records only *why*.

Why there is **no virtual filesystem**, which was the proposal and is the wrong direction:

- **It would increase privilege in the name of reducing it.** Caching needs to read byte ranges and to put and
  get opaque keys. A filesystem abstraction adds paths that can be traversed, handles that can be raced, and
  permissions that can be misconfigured — authority the function never uses.
- **The narrowness is the security property.** A keyed store with no paths has no path to construct, so path
  traversal does not exist as a class of defect; a write-once store cannot be altered between check and use.
- **It was already anticipated.** The decision behind [RFC-0004](../rfc/RFC-0004.md) records interfaces growing toward a general
  filesystem as a drift to watch, so declining it here is consistency rather than a new position.

Why a byte cache is a **decorator rather than a layer**: because retrieval is defined as explicit offset and
length with batched multi-range support, a cache is simply an implementation of that interface wrapping
another. Coalescing and deduplication become portable logic, the backing store stays host-supplied, and a
consumer cannot tell a caching source from a non-caching one.

Why decoded entries are keyed **per attribute**: [RFC-0002:C-PROJECTION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-projection) otherwise forces a choice between
fragmenting the cache per distinct projection and caching whole records, which discards the benefit projection
exists for. Caching each decoded attribute separately and assembling a batch on demand avoids both, and
sharing across pipelines with differing projections then requires no special handling.

Why integrity is verified **only on the committed path**:

- **The consequences are not comparable.** A tampered entry serving a preview costs a wrong pixel. The same
  entry serving a committed run costs a wrong delivered measurement.
- **The cost lands where it hurts most.** Verifying every read puts a digest over every cached byte range on
  the interactive path, the only path with a frame budget, to protect output
  [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-preview) 1 already forbids anyone from keeping.
- **It is the split already used five times.** Strictness where a result is kept, latitude where it is not.

Why failure is a **cache miss and not an error**: [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 4 and [RFC-0004:C-CACHE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-cache) 1 guarantee
every entry is re-derivable, so discarding and re-deriving is always available. Treating verification failure
as an error would turn a recoverable condition into an interruption, and would tempt an implementation to skip
verification to avoid spurious failures.

The obligation is detection, not prevention. Nothing here stops an entry being altered; the guarantee is that
an altered entry cannot silently contribute to a delivered result — the same standard
[RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) applies to a substituted source.

## Consequences

### Positive

Caching needs no new capability, so the privilege surface does not grow — and on a constrained host the same
cache code works against browser-resident storage as against a disk, because neither paths nor handles were
ever assumed. A byte cache is interchangeable with a plain source, so caching can be added or removed
without a consumer noticing. Per-attribute keying makes cache sharing automatic across pipelines that read
different attribute sets. And a stated guarantee — that consolidation cannot change results — becomes
enforceable rather than aspirational.

### Negative

Two verification regimes exist, so whether an entry is serving a committed run must be known at the point of
use rather than inferred later. Every entry carries a digest, which costs storage and a hash on write even
where it is never verified.

A tampered entry can still affect a preview, and therefore what a user believes they are looking at. That is
accepted rather than overlooked: [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-preview) 1 forbids a preview being kept or exported, so the
cost is a wrong pixel and cannot become a wrong delivered measurement.

### Neutral

Three drifts to watch. First, the storage interface acquiring paths or handles because a cache
implementation would find them convenient — the drift [ADR-0004](../adr/ADR-0004.md) already names, arriving disguised as
ergonomics. Second, verification being skipped on the committed path under performance pressure, which would
silently unenforce [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 2 while every existing test continues to pass. Third, verification
failure being surfaced as an error because a silent cache miss looks like hidden behaviour — that would push
implementers toward disabling verification, which is the opposite of the intent, and is why
[RFC-0004:C-INTEGRITY](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-integrity) 3 routes the signal into the evaluation configuration instead.

Reversal cost is low in the direction of strengthening and high in the direction of loosening. Widening
verification to every read later is additive. Narrowing it, or adding a filesystem abstraction, are the
changes that cost — the first weakens a delivered-result guarantee, the second expands privilege in a way
every host implementation would then depend on.

## Alternatives Considered

### Caches are decorators over the existing host interfaces, keyed per attribute, carrying a content digest verified only where an entry contributes to a committed run (accepted)

- **Pros:** No new capability or interface — the two host interfaces already suffice, Narrow interfaces are the security property: no paths to traverse, no in-place modification to race, A byte cache implementing the retrieval interface makes caching and non-caching sources interchangeable, Per-attribute keying avoids both projection fragmentation and whole-record waste, Verification cost lands off the interactive path, which is the only path with a frame budget, Verification failure degrades to a cache miss, since every entry is re-derivable by construction
- **Cons:** Two verification regimes, so which path an entry serves must be known at use time, A tampered entry can still affect a preview, and therefore what a user believes they are seeing

### Introduce a virtual filesystem abstraction for cache storage, with paths and handles, implemented per host (rejected)

- **Pros:** Familiar shape that most developers can implement without reading a specification, Directory structure gives cache organisation and inspection for free, One abstraction serves caching, spill, configuration and export
- **Cons:** Paths, traversal, handles and permissions are strictly more authority than caching needs, Path handling reintroduces traversal as a class of defect that a keyed store cannot have, Seekable handles cannot be implemented where retrieval is request-shaped
- **Rejected because:** It increases privilege in the name of reducing attack surface. Caching needs to read byte ranges and to put and get opaque keys, both already specified; a filesystem abstraction adds paths that can be traversed, handles that can be raced, and permissions to get wrong. The decision behind [RFC-0004](../rfc/RFC-0004.md) already recorded exactly this growth as a drift to watch.

### Verify the digest of every cache entry on every read, regardless of path (rejected)

- **Pros:** One rule, no regime boundary, and no need to know which path an entry serves, A tampered entry cannot affect even what a user sees on screen
- **Cons:** Places a digest over every cached byte range on the interactive path, Protects output that [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-preview) 1 already forbids anyone from keeping
- **Rejected because:** It pays the whole verification cost on the one path that has a frame budget, to protect results that may not be kept or exported. A tampered entry serving a preview costs a wrong pixel; the same entry serving a committed run costs a wrong delivered measurement, and only the latter warrants the cost.

### No integrity verification: rely on the source fingerprint alone to detect problems (rejected)

- **Pros:** Zero cost on every path; simplest possible implementation, Fingerprints already detect the common case of a source having been replaced
- **Cons:** A fingerprint detects staleness, not modification of the cache entry itself, A tampered baked overlay would change a delivered result while [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 2 asserts it cannot
- **Rejected because:** It leaves a stated guarantee unenforced. [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake) 2 asserts that consolidation cannot change results, and without entry integrity a modified overlay does exactly that, silently, with the provenance trail recording that nothing was wrong. A digest is cheap where it is required and re-derivation makes failure recoverable.
